Medical Dermatology in Jaipur | Skin Tags, Warts, Moles & Skin Problems

Skin tags, warts and moles are very common, and most are harmless. At Kezza, a doctor examines each growth first, then removes skin tags, warts and harmless raised moles with radiofrequency under local anaesthetic. A mole that looks unusual is not burned off: it needs surgical removal and laboratory testing. We also see common skin problems such as rashes, eczema and fungal infections at our Jaipur, Sikar and Ajmer clinics.

What We Cover

What Does Medical Dermatology at Kezza Cover?

At Kezza, medical dermatology covers the removal of skin tags, warts and harmless moles, and treatment of common skin problems such as rashes, eczema and fungal infections. Every growth is examined by a doctor first, and anything that looks unusual is sent for laboratory testing rather than removed for appearance.

Skin tags are soft, skin-coloured growths that hang from the skin on a small stalk, usually on the neck, armpits, eyelids, under the breasts or in the groin. They are harmless and become more common with age, friction from skin folds or jewellery, excess weight, type 2 diabetes and pregnancy. People usually have them removed because they catch on clothes or chains, bleed when rubbed or bother them.

Warts are rough growths caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV). They are contagious until they have gone, and although they often clear by themselves, this can take months or even years. Moles are clusters of pigment cells. Most are harmless and stay the same for years, but a mole that changes, bleeds or looks different from your others needs a doctor's attention.

Radiofrequency removal uses a very fine electrode that delivers controlled heat to remove the growth and seal small blood vessels. It suits skin tags, warts and selected raised moles that a doctor is confident are harmless. It is not used for moles that need testing, because the heat leaves no tissue sample to examine.

In Short:

  • Checked first: every growth is examined before removal.
  • Quick procedure: local anaesthetic, home the same day.
  • Tested when needed: unusual moles are sent to a lab, not burned off.

Suitability

Is Removal or Treatment Right for You?

Most skin tags, warts and harmless moles can be removed safely once a doctor has checked them.

Book a visit if

  • You have skin tags that catch on clothes or jewellery, or that you would like removed
  • You have common warts on your hands, feet or face that have not cleared
  • You have a raised mole that bothers you and want a doctor to check whether removal is suitable
  • You have a rash, itch, patch or infection that has not settled with simple care

Tell us, or get urgent care, if

  • A mole is changing, bleeding, itching or looks different from your other moles: it needs examination and testing, not cosmetic removal
  • You have warts in the genital area: please see a sexual health clinic
  • You have a pacemaker or implanted defibrillator: tell the doctor before any radiofrequency treatment
  • You form raised (keloid) scars easily, or take blood-thinning medicines
  • You have a fever with a rash, or a rash that is spreading fast, blistering or affecting your eyes, mouth or genitals: seek urgent medical care

Please do not cut, burn or tie off skin growths at home, or use 'mole remover' creams. The US Food and Drug Administration has received reports of scarring and infections from such products, and they can delay the diagnosis of skin cancer.

Procedure

How Removal Works

Most removals take a few minutes, after the examination and consent.

01

Examination

The doctor examines the growth in good light, asks how long you have had it and whether it has changed, and checks your other moles if needed.

02

Plan & Consent

You hear which method suits it, what mark it may leave, the chance of it returning and the cost, before you decide.

03

Numbing

A small injection of local anaesthetic numbs the area, so you feel pressure and warmth rather than pain.

04

Removal

Radiofrequency removes the skin tag, wart or harmless mole and seals small blood vessels. Unusual moles are removed surgically for testing instead.

05

Dressing & Aftercare

The area is dressed and you get written care instructions. Small wounds usually heal in one to three weeks.

Healing

Healing After Removal

Healing time depends on the size and site of the growth.

D1

Same Day

A small scab forms over the treated spot; you go home straight away.

D3

First Few Days

Keep the area clean and dry as advised, apply the recommended ointment and do not pick the scab.

W2

One to Three Weeks

Most small wounds heal and the scab falls off on its own.

M2

Following Months

The spot may look pink, lighter or darker for a few months; sunscreen helps it settle.

M3

Review

Warts are checked again, because some come back and need another treatment.

Medical Note: Results vary from person to person. This page is general information from Kezza Hair & Skin Clinic and is not a substitute for a consultation with a doctor.

Moles: when to get one checked

Most moles are harmless, but melanoma, a serious skin cancer, can start in a mole or look like a new one. The ABCDE signs help: Asymmetry, an irregular Border, uneven Colour, a Diameter usually larger than 6 mm, and Evolving, meaning any change in size, shape or colour. A mole that itches, bleeds or looks different from your other moles should also be examined. In darker skin, skin cancer is often found late, and it can appear on the palms, soles, nails or inside the mouth, or as a sore that does not heal.

When a mole looks unusual, the right treatment is surgical removal with a margin of normal skin, followed by laboratory examination. Lasers, cautery and freezing are not used for these moles, because they leave no tissue to examine, and Indian guidelines on radiofrequency surgery note that heat damage can interfere with laboratory testing. For raised moles that are clearly harmless, removal for comfort or appearance is possible, but it can leave a mark, and moles removed by shaving or radiofrequency are more likely to grow back than those cut out completely.

Warts: treatment and recurrence

Warts are spread by touch and by sharing towels or footwear. Many clear without treatment, so for a small wart that does not bother you, waiting is reasonable. When treatment is wanted, options include salicylic acid, freezing, radiofrequency (electrosurgery) and scraping. After electrosurgery, healing usually takes two weeks or longer, around one in five warts comes back within a few months, and a small scar is possible. Warts on the soles may need several sessions. Genital warts are different: they need assessment at a sexual health clinic, and pharmacy wart treatments should not be used on them.

Skin tags: safe removal

Skin tags are not dangerous and do not turn into cancer, so removal is a personal choice. They can be removed with heat (radiofrequency or cautery), by freezing or by snipping them off with a sterile blade or scissors. Larger tags or those on the eyelids need extra care. Tying them off with thread, cutting them at home or using removal creams risks infection, bleeding and scars. A doctor also makes sure that what looks like a skin tag is not another kind of growth.

Common skin problems we see

Alongside growths, many people come with long-term skin problems. Eczema cannot be cured, but treatment can control itching and flares. Psoriasis is not contagious and is a long-term condition managed with medical treatment. Fungal infections such as ringworm need an antifungal used every day for up to four weeks, even after the rash fades. In India, steroid creams sold without prescription, often mixed with antifungals, are a major cause of stubborn, widespread ringworm, so we avoid them and help you stop them safely. If your condition needs specialist care, we will tell you and refer you.

Some rashes need urgent care rather than a clinic appointment: a rash with fever, a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, blistering, a rash that spreads quickly or one that affects the eyes, mouth or genitals. A growth that bleeds, crusts or has not healed for more than four weeks should also be seen promptly.

Aftercare after removal

  • Keep the dressing on for the time advised, then clean the area gently and apply the recommended ointment.
  • Let the scab fall off on its own; picking it increases the risk of a mark.
  • Avoid swimming pools, saunas and heavy sweating until the skin has healed.
  • Use sunscreen on healed skin for a few months to help pink or dark marks settle.
  • Contact the clinic if you notice increasing redness, swelling, pus, fever or bleeding that does not stop with pressure.

Why patients choose Kezza for skin growths and skin problems

  • Checked before removal: a doctor examines every growth first and tells you plainly what it is.
  • Testing when it matters: moles that look unusual are sent for laboratory examination rather than removed for appearance.
  • Fine-tip technique: radiofrequency removal under local anaesthetic, with aftercare to help the skin heal well.
  • Three clinics: Jaipur, Sikar and Ajmer, open 9 AM to 8 PM every day.
  • Clear costs: the method and the cost, including any laboratory test, are explained before the procedure.

What affects the cost of removal?

The cost depends on how many growths are removed, their size and site, the method used and whether laboratory testing is needed. Removing a few small skin tags in one visit costs less than treating several warts over more than one session. The doctor explains the total before the procedure.

FAQs

Frequently Asked Questions

Will a skin tag come back after removal?
A skin tag that has been removed does not usually come back, but new tags can form elsewhere, especially in areas of friction. If you get new ones, they can be removed in the same way.
Can I remove a skin tag or mole at home?
No. The NHS advises against removing skin tags yourself because of the risk of infection, bleeding and scarring, and the US Food and Drug Administration has warned that products sold for removing moles and skin tags can cause skin injuries and delay the diagnosis of skin cancer.
Do warts go away without treatment?
Often, yes, but it can take months or even years, and they remain contagious until they have gone. Treatment is worth considering if a wart is painful, spreading or bothering you. Even after treatment, some warts come back and need a repeat session.
How do I know if a mole is dangerous?
Doctors use the ABCDE signs: Asymmetry, an irregular Border, more than one Colour, a Diameter usually over 6 mm and Evolving, meaning any change. A mole that itches, bleeds or looks different from your others should be checked. In brown skin, also watch for dark spots on the palms, soles or nails and sores that do not heal.
Will radiofrequency removal leave a scar?
It can leave a small mark. The treated skin may look lighter or darker for a few months, and darker skin is more prone to temporary darkening. People who form keloids are more likely to scar. The doctor explains what to expect for your skin and the site before you decide.
Is radiofrequency removal painful?
A local anaesthetic is used, so most people feel only the small injection and then some warmth or pressure. The area may feel sore for a day or two afterwards; simple pain relief is usually enough.
Why does my ringworm keep coming back?
Common reasons are stopping the antifungal treatment too early and using creams that contain a steroid. The NHS advises using antifungal treatment every day for up to four weeks, even after the rash has gone, and Indian experts link steroid cream misuse to the current rise in stubborn ringworm.
How long does healing take after wart or skin tag removal?
Small skin tags usually heal within one to two weeks. Warts removed with radiofrequency can take two weeks or longer, depending on their size and site. Keep the area clean, follow the aftercare advice and protect it from the sun while it heals.
